info.bio: Happy Mondays son una banda de rock alternativo formada en 1981 en Manchester, Inglaterra. Junto a bandas como The Stone Roses, The Charlatans, Joy Division o New Order entre otras, lideraron la escena musical denominada "madchester". La escena mezclaba el rock psicodélico, el indie y la música dance. Para fines de los 80s los Happy Mondays habían alcanzado cierta popularidad con discos como '24 Hour Party People' y 'Bummed', pero llegarían definitivamente a la cima con su tercer LP 'Pills N' Thrills N' Bellyaches' (1990)

scenes.name: Madchester y ambient house
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Un movimiento de Manchester que marca la música de baile como ningún otro de los ochenta: la fusión de psicodelia, techno y pop. KLF importa el acid house; los Stone Roses mezclan ritmos disco hipnóticos, melodías pegadizas y entusiasmo sesentero; los Happy Mondays de Shaun Ryder (Bummed) y Black Grape; Charlatans, Nitzer Ebb, Shamen, Pop Will Eat Itself, Jesus Jones. Más allá de la moda, 808 State (herederos de Kraftwerk, «Pacific State»), William Orbit, Richard Kirk, A Guy Called Gerald, el collage de Coldcut y Primal Scream (Screamadelica).
scenes.family: Soul, funk, disco, hip hop y baile

scenes.name: Mánchester: la Haçienda y Madchester
scenes.book: Techno Rebels: The Renegades of Electronic Funk
scenes.author: Dan Sicko
scenes.desc: En 1988, fuera del círculo de Rhythm King, había que ir a Mánchester para oír discos de Detroit: en la Haçienda (financiada por New Order) Mike Pickering, criado en el soul, pinchaba «Goodbye Kiss», «Groovin’ without a Doubt» o «Triangle of Love» antes que nadie en Londres, donde en el Spectrum no sonaban. La ciudad de los Smiths, The Fall y New Order unió el indie al acid house con los Happy Mondays, los Stone Roses e Inspiral Carpets, un puente hacia 808 State y A Guy Called Gerald.

podcast.title: 1988 Publications
podcast.body: Happy Mondays had significant publications around 1988 that contributed to the explosion of Manchester's danceable music. "también tenemos la publicación del material de los Happy Mondays"

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: John Peel Sessions (Spring 1988)
podcast.body: John Peel, a pivotal figure in modern music, featured Happy Mondays in Peel Sessions during the spring of 1988. These sessions were instrumental in disseminating the Manchester movement throughout the United Kingdom. "cuando John Pill saca pilsesiones de los Happy Mondays de los Stone Roses y de todas estas bandas ya pues incluso tenemos sesiones en música, Jaws, Guy Collierad, en la spillsession que era algo muy raro de ver, ya eso se es parce por todo el Reino Unido."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Decline of Manchester Sound (Early 1993)
podcast.body: The Manchester Sound, exemplified by the Happy Mondays, was "on the way out" by February 1993, coinciding with the spread of American Grunge causing a crisis in British music. "the Manchester Sound of the Stone Roses and the Happy Mondays was on the way out"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Acknowledging the End of Their Peak
podcast.body: During the chaotic "Yes Please" recording sessions in Barbados, the band members realized they had "peaked" and were merely "milking it," recognizing that their level of "goofiness" signaled the approaching end of their initial success. "So at some point, we knew he was ending... we've peaked. Yeah. And now we're just milking it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Acting and Composing Career
podcast.body: In later years, Paul Ryder branched out into acting and composed music for TV shows. "In later years he also became an actor and composer of music for TV shows."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: In Memoriam of Those Lost in 2022

podcast.title: Baggy Trousers Style Origin
podcast.body: The band's distinctive "baggy pants" fashion, characterized by cheap, flared trousers, originated from their manager, Phil Sacks. As an original Northern Soul DJ who owned a shop, Phil Sacks sold these types of clothes, which the band adopted and integrated into their look. "But we used to go with Phil Sacks at a shop and became our manager. And he was the original Northern Soul DJ. And he was selling him."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Band Entourage in Barbados
podcast.body: The Happy Mondays' recording session in Barbados involved a large entourage, swelling to about 30 people at one point as families, including Gazz Wheeling's wife, came to stay near the studio. "We were part of about 30 people at one point."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Band Formation and Learning Instruments
podcast.body: The Happy Mondays formed in 1982 when Gaz Wheelan was still at school. Like many UK bands, they adopted the approach of forming a band first and then learning their instruments over several years, a contrast to the North American method of learning instruments before forming a band. "We formed 82 when I was still... Oh, I was still at school, I was still really old. And nothing really happened for years, did it? What was really funny about... No, because the difference between UK and North America with bands is, in the UK, you form a band, then learn your instruments."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Band Recoupment for Damages
podcast.body: The band ultimately had to pay for all damages and expenses incurred during the Barbados recording, including the car crashes, as these costs were recouped from them by the label. "The bandled up paying for everything, don't they?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Oral History of Manchester Part 2

podcast.title: Barbados Album Budget Misuse
podcast.body: While recording an album in Barbados, the band spent their entire allocated budget on drugs instead of producing the record properly. "When labelhead Tony Wilson allowed the band to record an album in Barbados, they spent their entire budget on drugs instead of making a proper record."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Barbados Album Recording Chaos
podcast.body: The recording of their follow-up album, "Yes Please," in Barbados at Eddy Grant's studio was marked by extreme chaos and excess. The band and their families, a party of about 30 people, were on the remote, non-tourist Atlantic side of the island, which contributed to the uncontrolled environment. "It didn't go well at all."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Oral History of Manchester Part 2

podcast.title: Barbados Recording Session Chaos - Bez's Jeep Incident
podcast.body: During the Barbados sessions, Bez had a Jeep and drove it into the marshlands near the studio's pool. The Jeep ended up upside down, crushing Bez and resulting in him having "all these pins and his arm." Approximately two weeks later, Bez broke his arm again attempting to jet ski. "this Jeep upside down and he was crushed and he had all these pins and his arm and then two days, I know, I know about two weeks after he was, you know, trying to try to jet ski in the yellow, you know, and broke it again."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Barbados Recording Session Chaos - Car Destruction
podcast.body: While recording in Barbados, the band was involved in numerous car accidents, with "more than nine" cars reportedly destroyed due to the poor road conditions, particularly on the less touristy east side where Eddie Grant's studio was located. "I think it was about, I thought it was nine, but then someone told me it was more."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Barbados Recording Session Chaos - Crack Den at the Studio Pool
podcast.body: Studio staff, including a man named Mark from New York, discovered that the band had transformed the sun lounges by the studio pool into a makeshift crack den, a situation Gazz Wheeling found "hilarious." "I went up to the pool and they turned the sun lounges... they turned and they made a track down out of it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Barbados Recording Session Chaos - Sam Lord's Castle Incident
podcast.body: During the recording of their "Yes Please" album in Barbados, the band stayed at Sam Lord's Castle. On their first night, after a long flight, the keyboard player, PDR, got drunk, became annoyed by a cabaret band called "Spice" or "Spice Boys," got on stage, and was subsequently escorted away by the police, leading to the band being kicked out of the castle. "He'd got so annoyed that I hated the cabaret band that he'd got up stage and it's like one of them. That's how it all started."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Barbados Recording Session Chaos - Shaun Ryder Crashes into Bar
podcast.body: One night, while Gazz Wheeling was drinking at a small, shack-like bar, Shaun Ryder drove a car straight through the front of the establishment, asking for Gazz. The bar owner, a former West Indian cricketer, was wealthy and calmly stated he would pay for the damage, as did the band. "This car comes through the front, the front bit of the bar... And everyone jumped up and then show mocks instead of heard you was here."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Barbados Recording Session Disaster – Collapse of Factory Records
podcast.body: The Happy Mondays' drug binge in Barbados during the recording of their album proved catastrophic for Factory Records in the early 1990s. Band members consumed crack at a staggering rate, destroyed cars, a member broke his arm, and they sold their own possessions to fund drug purchases. They delivered an album devoid of lyrics and vocals. The incident directly accelerated the financial ruin of Factory Records. "Destroyed cars, a member broke his arm, and sold their belongings to buy drugs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bez's Collaboration with Joe Strummer
podcast.body: Bez, a former member of Happy Mondays, was involved in an unsuccessful attempt to collaborate with Joe Strummer on a new band project after Strummer's record label dispute. "then Joe tried to get something going with Bez, X of the Happy Mondays, but that didn't work out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bez's Crack-Related Injury
podcast.body: Dancer Bez sustained serious injuries, including a severely busted right arm that required an external metal brace for weeks, which was attributed to his crack cocaine use. "And Baaz got into accidents that busted up his right arm so badly that he had to wear an external metal brace for weeks. And you can blame that on crack, the most addictive form of cocaine."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bez's Favorite Album
podcast.body: Despite its chaotic production and perceived failure by some, "Yes Please" is Bez's favorite Happy Mondays album. "it's best his favorite album."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Oral History of Manchester Part 2

podcast.title: Bez's Jeep Accident and Injuries
podcast.body: During the Barbados sessions, Bez crushed himself in a Jeep accident in the marshlands near the studio. He sustained serious arm injuries requiring pins but was reportedly jet-skiing and re-injuring it just two weeks later. "Bez with his arm in some kind of, he was, uh, medical device... he was crushed and he had all these pins and his arm."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Oral History of Manchester Part 2

podcast.title: Car Crash into Bar
podcast.body: One night in Barbados, after Gazz Wheeling finished drumming, he witnessed a car crash directly through the front of a small shack bar where he was drinking. The car was driven by an ex-West Indian cricketer, who immediately offered to pay for the damages. "this car comes through the front, the front bit of the bar... The car drove into the bar."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Oral History of Manchester Part 2

podcast.title: Car Destruction in Barbados
podcast.body: During their Barbados recording session for "Yes Please," multiple cars were destroyed due to reckless behavior and poor road conditions on the island's east side. Estimates for the number of destroyed cars vary from nine to "more." "how many cars were destroyed? ... I thought it was nine, but then someone told me it was more."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Oral History of Manchester Part 2

podcast.title: Cause of Death: Ischemic Heart Disease
podcast.body: The cause of Paul Ryder's death was ischemic heart disease with complications of diabetes. "Cause of death, ischemic heart disease with complications of diabetes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: In Memoriam of Those Lost in 2022

podcast.title: Chaotic Lifestyle
podcast.body: The Happy Mondays were known for their wild and chaotic lifestyle, marked by extensive drug and alcohol abuse and numerous "stupid escapades." "the happy Mondays were a real piece of work. In fact, I could probably do an entire stupid history episode on them alone. So many drugs, so much alcohol, so many stupid escapades."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Coined "Madchester" Term
podcast.body: The Happy Mondays are credited with coming up with the term "Madchester," which they featured in their November 1989 single "Madchester Rave On." "They also deserve credit for coming up with a term madchester."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: Control Room Couch Traded for Drugs
podcast.body: During the recording of their fourth album in Barbados, singer Shaun Ryder and Bez famously traded the control room couch from the studio for drugs. "And the couch from the control room at the studio disappeared because Sean and Bez traded it for drugs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Discovered by Tony Wilson
podcast.body: This band was discovered by Tony Wilson, who was also instrumental in the Manchester movement. "El descubrió a los Habimondas."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Especial JOY DIVISION: 4. La banda tras el final

podcast.title: Discovery by Tony Wilson
podcast.body: Tony Wilson, the founder of Factory Records, is credited with discovering Happy Mondays (referred to as "los capi-mondes"), highlighting their importance as a part of the Manchester movement. "Tony Wilson... también con la que descubriría los capi-mondes y una parte importante de este movimiento Manchester"

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Drug-Related Decline
podcast.body: The band was "too stone to do anything" during Madchester's golden period, indicating that drug use contributed to their inactivity and the scene's burnout. "The Happy Mondays were too stone to do anything."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: Early Image and Influence on Lad Culture
podcast.body: Around 1985, Happy Mondays' casual image, characterized by wearing trainers and "regular" shirts, was questioned by record labels seeking a defined look. The band refused to change, and this style, which they had cultivated for years, later became a foundational element of "lad culture" that emerged approximately a decade later. "And they came up and they were like, what's your image? And we was like, well, this is how we dress. And they were like, well, what you wear in trainers and getting images like, you know, we're not wearing, you know, this is how we dress."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Local Popularity and Delayed Recordings
podcast.body: Before achieving widespread recognition, Happy Mondays, along with bands like James and The Stone Roses, were giving numerous local concerts in Manchester and had released small singles within the city between 1982 and 1984. They were "authentic idols" in Manchester but took years to record substantial material due to their "completely carefree" nature, a trait that proved incompatible with the demands of major labels later on. "pensé que el mejor osestón Rose o James o los capi-mondes no eran famosos pero sí que ya estaban dando muchos conciertos locales en Manchester ya tenían pequeñas cosas sacadas en síngles dentro de la ciudad de Manchester"

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Early Popularity in London vs. Manchester
podcast.body: The Happy Mondays found significant success and were filling small venues in London a full year before they achieved similar recognition in their hometown of Manchester. They struggled to gain airplay or positive reviews in Manchester, where critics often "didn't get what was going on" with their music, unlike the London press. "Well, we were big in London before we were big in Manchester."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Recognition
podcast.body: The speaker recalled reading about the Happy Mondays and immediately recognizing their potential to become a significant band. The radio station's staff enthusiastically supported their music, believing they were leading the culture in Toronto, Ontario, Western New York, and possibly beyond, particularly for British music. "I remember reading about the Happy Mondays and thinking, okay, this band is going to be something along with the stone roses and the charlatans."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: OGHONM 1000th Episode: The Q&A From the Live Recording

podcast.title: Ecstasy Introduction at The Haçienda
podcast.body: The Ryder brothers played a significant role in introducing ecstasy to the crowd at The Haçienda, the Manchester nightclub co-owned by New Order and Factory Records. "led by the writer brothers who had a big part in introducing ecstasy to the crowd at the Haseyenda, the Manchester Nightclub co-owned by New Order in factory records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: Essence Compromised by Major Labels
podcast.body: The band's "carefree" approach, which led them to spend years performing locally as idols without quickly producing recorded material, was incompatible with the commercial pressures of major multinational labels. These labels, in their rush to capitalize on the Manchester sound, ultimately "destroyed" the movement's authentic essence. "no olvidemos que grupos como los Estón Rosos o como los JAPY mondesis tuvieron años en Manchester dando con ciertos y siendo muy populares y indoténticos ídolos en la ciudad sin grabar material porque ellos eran gente completamente dejada entonces no era muy compatible todo esto con las grandes multinacionales y al final puesto a estas multinacionales se lo acabaron cargando."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Extensive Drug Habits
podcast.body: The Happy Mondays were known for their significant use of ecstasy, cocaine, heroin, and crack, with their drug habits ultimately leading to the demise of their record label, Factory Records. "Not only were they big users of ecstasy, but also cocaine and heroin and even crack. Their drug habits killed their record label factory records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Factory Records Bankruptcy Myth
podcast.body: The band did not bankrupt Factory Records, a claim often associated with them. Instead, Factory Records owed the Happy Mondays a substantial amount of money when the label went under, with the bankruptcy attributed to bad management. "No, we didn't. That's another myth. We didn't."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Oral History of Manchester Part 2

podcast.title: Factory Records Bankruptcy Myth
podcast.body: The band refutes the myth that they were responsible for bankrupting Factory Records. Instead, they assert that the label went under due to "bad management" and, upon its disbandment, Factory Records still owed the Happy Mondays a significant amount of money. "No, we didn't. That's another myth. We didn't."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Factory Records Collapse – No Legal Contracts with Artists
podcast.body: Factory Records' attempt to sell its assets to London Records was derailed when it was discovered that the label held no legally binding contracts with any of its artists. This fundamental structural flaw made the label impossible to sell and hastened its complete collapse. "They had no legally binding contracts with their artists."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Factory Records Contract
podcast.body: Contrary to popular myth, Happy Mondays did have a contract with Factory Records, though it might have been an unusual arrangement that allowed them considerable freedom. Tony Wilson, head of Factory Records, loved the band and let them operate with this leeway, despite much of the rest of the label, including other bands and managers, not taking to them. "We did have a contract... Tony loved us. Everyone hated us."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Factory Records Contract
podcast.body: Contrary to a common perception that Factory Records bands lacked formal contracts, the Happy Mondays confirmed they did have a contract. The label, particularly Tony Wilson, granted them considerable artistic freedom, allowing them to "do what we want." "No, we did. We had a concert, but they would pray. They would let us do what we want."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Food Health Discussions on Tour Bus
podcast.body: During their reunion tour, members like Gaz and Rovetta would engage in discussions on the tour bus about healthy eating, railing against "the evils of eating pork and processed foods and having too much meat," which was a stark contrast to their past image. "The rest of us sat in the dining area, listening to gas and rovetta, rail above the evils of eating pork and processed foods and having too much meat."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Founding Member and Madchester Era Force
podcast.body: Paul Ryder was a founding member of the Happy Mondays, and the group became a major force during the Madchester era of the early 1990s. "Paul Ryder with the happy Mondays. He was a founding member of the group which became a major force during the Madchester era of the very early 1990s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: In Memoriam of Those Lost in 2022

podcast.title: Gaz Whelan's Relocation to Burlington, Ontario
podcast.body: The band's drummer, Gaz Whelan, relocated from Manchester to Burlington, Ontario, a decision prompted by his wife's interest in Canada after seeing it featured on a real estate television show. Whelan was described as "totally straight, totally sober" during the reunion period. "I'd made the acquaintance of Gas Wheelan, the band's drummer who would relocate it to Burlington, Ontario."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Stop Me If You've Heard This One Before

podcast.title: Gazz Wheeling's Barbados Activities
podcast.body: During the Barbados recording sessions for "Yes Please," drummer Gazz Wheeling finished recording his parts in the first week. Subsequently, he spent his time drinking local rum and self-medicating with local herb, enjoying the chaotic environment from a distance while his wife and other families joined the party. "I was drinking a lot of, a lot of local rum. I was, uh, self-medicating with a lot of local herb."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Oral History of Manchester Part 2

podcast.title: Gazz Wheeling's Departure
podcast.body: Gazz Wheeling decided to leave the Happy Mondays after a tour in Australia because Shaun Ryder was cutting set times to as little as 20 minutes, despite headlining festivals requiring 90-minute sets, and expecting to be paid to record new music. Wheeling felt Shaun Ryder was doing "what he wanted to do," and there was mutual fatigue among the members. "Sean, you know, was cutting the set, so he wanted to do 20 minutes... he'd pay me to come in the studio to do recordings."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Oral History of Manchester Part 2

podcast.title: Gazz Wheeling's Departure
podcast.body: Gazz Wheeling ultimately left the Happy Mondays because of Shaun Ryder's behavior, which included cutting live sets down to 20 minutes (even at festivals expecting 1.5 hours) and having to be paid to show up for recording sessions for a new album. Gazz felt the new material wasn't as good as their early work, and Shaun's actions made continued collaboration difficult. "I knew I had to leave one to come straight on the other and they got to the point where Sean, you know, was cutting the sets."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Initial Resistance from Factory Records
podcast.body: When Happy Mondays were signed to Factory Records, there was some initial skepticism and resistance from certain factions within the label, who reportedly referred to them as "football hooligans" due to their appearance. Despite this, they were allowed to perform on the label's premises to generate interest, implying Tony Wilson's support. "And I think when we went on factory, there was a lot of, by the long Colt Brigade on factories, like, you know, not them, you know."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Kicked Out of Sam Lord's Castle
podcast.body: On their first night in Barbados, the band was kicked out of Sam Lord's Castle, their initial accommodation. This happened after their keyboard player, PDR, assaulted a member of a cabaret band called Spice or The Spice Boys due to annoyance, leading to his escort by police. "the first night we arrived, we stayed at this place called Sam Lod's castle... we got kicked out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Musical Style - House vs. Pop
podcast.body: Their sound leaned more towards house than pop, characterized by heavier beats, soulful melodies, and dense lyrics. "They were more house than pop with heavier beats and the melodies were more soulful and the lyrics were more dense."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: Musical Uniqueness and Influences
podcast.body: The Happy Mondays developed a completely unique sound, deliberately avoiding sounding like any one artist because they listened to a vast range of genres and artists, from Johnny Cash and Sly & The Family Stone to the Sex Pistols, The Band, William Ellison, The Rolling Stones, and The Beatles. This eclectic listening, coupled with their own perceived lack of traditional musical proficiency, resulted in a distinctive groove. "We just listened to everything. We didn't try it at the anyone, because we couldn't be, we weren't good enough."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Name Choice as Counterpoint
podcast.body: Almost a decade after Ian Curtis's death, another Manchester band, the Happy Mondays, deliberately chose their name to "counteract all that gloom," providing a stylistic and thematic contrast to the dark aesthetic of Joy Division. "And almost a decade later, another Manchester bad tried to counteract all that gloom by naming themselves the Happy Mondays."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

podcast.title: Origin of "Madchester" Term
podcast.body: The term "Madchester" was coined by "two lots of new castles" who had heard the Happy Mondays' music and videos. It became strongly associated with their "Madchester Rave On EP," particularly stemming from the EP's title, which was hastily chosen as "Rave On" from a comment about "All Night Where-outs parties." This led the press to link the music with "raves," creating the "Madchester" moniker. "That was coin by two lots of new castles who'd heard us."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 1000th Episode of the Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Reckless Behavior
podcast.body: The band engaged in destructive acts, such as driving a Jeep through the front door of a bar. "They also drove a Jeep through the front door of a bar."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rejoining and Touring with the Band
podcast.body: Paul Ryder had rejoined the Happy Mondays and was touring with them at the time of his death. "And then he rejoined the happy Mondays and was touring with him when he died."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Relationship with Factory Records Staff
podcast.body: Apart from Tony Wilson, who "loved" the Happy Mondays and supported them, many other bands, managers, and staff at Factory Records "hated" them or "didn't really take tools." "Tony Loved Us, everyone hated us."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Reunions Not for Tax Reasons
podcast.body: Shaun Ryder claimed the band reunited multiple times for tax reasons, but Gazz Wheeling stated this was a "safety net" to avoid appearing as if they genuinely wanted or needed to reunite, reflecting a "Mancunian" attitude of not showing enjoyment for commercial endeavors. "No, that was, that was just Sean saying that to kind of, ever, as a bit of a, a, a safety net in case it all went perjokes, just so it looked like we, the thing, well, it's kind of like not trying to look like we needed to get back all we wanted to."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Oral History of Manchester Part 2

podcast.title: Reunions and Shaun Ryder's Persona
podcast.body: The Happy Mondays reunited only once after an initial break, not multiple times for "tax reasons" as sometimes suggested. Gazz Wheeling clarified that Shaun Ryder used the "tax reasons" excuse as a "safety net" to maintain a "real Manchester finger" persona, where not "enjoying it" was considered "cool" and a reflection of a working-class English identity. "No, that was, that was just Sean saying that to kind of ever, as a bit of a, a safety net in case it all went pear-shaped."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Sean Ryder's Insecurity and Stage Presence
podcast.body: Sean Ryder, the band's singer, was considered insecure, a trait Gaz Wheelan attributes to many singers, partly because Sean "wasn't a textbook singer" and never claimed to be one. To compensate, the band frequently invited friends, including Bez, to dance on stage, which created a more dynamic and less exposed performance for Sean. "Sean was insecure, so he needed a crook, you know, on stage."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Shaun Ryder's Shyness and Insecurity
podcast.body: Despite his wild public persona, Shaun Ryder is described as being "shy" and "insecure." This hidden shyness, combined with the band's collective insecurities, was suggested to be a driving force behind some of their behavior, rooted in a working-class English mentality of "not getting above your station." "No, Sean was kind of, a little more Sean, yeah, it's shy, Sean, shy. So that's why he did it, you know, he was shy, basically, and we were kind of all kind of insecure."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Shaun Ryder's Unconventional Recording Process
podcast.body: Shaun Ryder typically did not get involved in the music composition, preferring to add lyrics later, often after the music for an entire album was written. For "Yes Please," he only contributed lyrics for one song, which was unusual even for his late-stage lyric writing habits. "he'd always did the lyrics later, he never got involved in the music, ever."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Oral History of Manchester Part 2

podcast.title: Shift to "Ultra-Cleaned Living Ways"
podcast.body: The band, famously associated with drugs, alcohol, and debauchery in the 90s (pot, coke, heroin, PCP, crack), underwent a drastic lifestyle change by the time of their reunion tour. Their tour bus was clean, smoke-free, drug-free, and alcohol-free, with only coffee and chocolate available, and wives and children often on board. "The happy Mondays from their baggy, drug-y days, it is not that way anymore. I am witness to their current ultra-cleaned living ways."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Stop Me If You've Heard This One Before

podcast.title: Signed by Rob Gretton to Factory Records
podcast.body: Happy Mondays were among the bands that signed with Factory Records thanks to the efforts of manager Rob Gretton. Gretton's keen eye for talent helped populate the cool new indie label with significant acts from the Manchester scene.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Sudden Death Before Kubix Festival
podcast.body: Paul Ryder died suddenly on July 15th at the age of 58. He had flown from Los Angeles to Manchester to play gigs with the band, complained of headaches upon arrival, went to bed, and was found by his mother the next morning, just hours before the band was scheduled to play the Kubix festival. "In July he flew in from his home in Los Angeles to play some gigs with the Mondays. When he arrived in Madchester he complained that he was having some headaches. He went to bed and never woke up. He was found by his mother on July 15th. Just hours before the band was supposed to play the Kubik's festival."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: In Memoriam of Those Lost in 2022

podcast.title: Sun Lounges as Crack Den
podcast.body: Band members converted sun loungers by the pool near Eddy Grant's studio in Barbados into a makeshift crack den, a place where many of them spent their time. "they turned the sun, the sun lounges... They turned and they made it cracked and out of it. It stopped open to a crack there."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Oral History of Manchester Part 2

podcast.title: UK Reunion Tour (2010s)
podcast.body: Against initial odds, the Happy Mondays reunited for a series of shows across the UK, signaling a significant return for the band known for its Madchester era excesses. The tour included a stop at Brixton Academy where Inspiral Carpets opened. "But, against all odds, the Mondays came back together for a series of shows across the UK."

podcast.title: US House Music Influence (Theory)
podcast.body: One theory posits that the initial arrival of House music in Manchester was facilitated by one or two members of the Happy Mondays, who spent time in the United States and brought back the first LPs of Chicago House music from New York and Chicago. "tenemos también la teoría de que sería uno de los miembros o un par de miembros de los capi-mondes que pasaron un tiempo en Estados Unidos, se habrían traído en Nueva York y de Chicago los primeros LPs de música House del movimiento House de Chicago"

xref.title: Early Interactions with Happy Mondays
xref.body: Gazz Wheeling and Kelly knew Noel Gallagher personally. Gazz recalls interviewing him "for a few drinks" in a downstairs area, noting a past conflict where Noel "had fallen out with Sean" (likely Shaun Ryder or a member of Inspiral Carpets) due to "words in his spirals." During this early interaction, Noel even offered to play drums for Happy Mondays if they ever needed someone. "He said, if you ever need anyone to do your drums, I'll do it."

xref.body: Emerging from Britain in the late 1980s, The Stone Roses became one of the most popular and influential bands of their time. "Out of all the bands to come out of Britain in the late 1980s, no one was more popular and influential than the Stone Roses."
